extracted.intended_audience: Journalists and contributors at Guardian News & Media (GNM) — staff, freelancers and editors
extracted.subtask_description: Organisation-level editorial and legal guidance for news gathering, verification, privacy, source protection, conflicts of interest, and professional conduct for Guardian News & Media journalists and contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy — intrusion must be justified by public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Where reporting or newsgathering may intrude on privacy, there must be proper prior consideration of the public interest and authorisation from the relevant senior duty editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The degree and method of any intrusion must be justified by the seriousness of the story and the public good likely to follow. Do not conduct “fishing” expeditions into people’s private lives unless the issue, suspicion and prospects of success are all serious. There may be circumstances where people can reasonably expect privacy even in public places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Photography and video footage
rubrics_metrics.description: Care when photographing or filming where an individual has a reasonable expectation of privacy, is unaware the picture/footage is being taken for publication, and/or has not provided consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider location and activity; use of long-lens photography is not prohibited but may be a relevant factor when assessing intrusion. See editorial code guidance section P on pictures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying details
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise caution about reporting and publishing identifying details that may enable others to intrude on the privacy or safety of people who have become the subject of media coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include street names and house numbers; consider potential for enabling third-party intrusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of the Omand principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Sir David Omand’s proportionality framework — five questions journalists should ask before intruding on privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1) Is there sufficient cause? The intrusion must be justified by the scale of potential harm. 2) Is there integrity of motive? The intrusion must be justified in terms of public benefit. 3) Will the methods be proportionate to the seriousness of the story and its public interest? 4) Is there proper authority? Intrusion must be authorised at a sufficiently senior level with appropriate oversight. 5) Is there a reasonable prospect of success? Fishing expeditions are not justified. Where there is a legitimate expectation of privacy, journalists/editors must be able to demonstrate why an infringement is justified in the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to reply
rubrics_metrics.description: Make every effort to contact the person or organisation that is the subject of a story before publication to put allegations to them and give them an opportunity to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assists accuracy, fairness and demonstrates consideration of public interest. Take account of complexity and time zones. The more serious the criticism or allegations, the greater the obligation to allow response. Editorial legal services can advise on best practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources — confidentiality and anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: When a source seeks anonymity or requests confidentiality, discuss the request with the relevant senior duty editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists have a moral obligation to protect confidential sources. Otherwise sources should be identified as specifically as possible. See clause 14 on confidential sources and related guidance on anonymous contributions and source care/protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing — social media
rubrics_metrics.description: GNM editorial code covers content published on social media as well as print and online platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before accessing, publishing or sharing material taken from social media or the wider internet, consider legal, copyright and ethical issues as with any other source. Familiarise with GNM’s social media guidelines and relevant professional behaviour guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subterfuge and covert behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should normally identify themselves as GNM employees when gathering material; subterfuge is a rare exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rare public interest exceptions must be approved in advance by the relevant senior duty editor and editorial legal consulted. Applies to hidden cameras/listening/recording devices and material obtained by subterfuge of others. If GNM is offered material obtained covertly by a third party, seek advice from the managing editor and editorial legal immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suicide and self-harm reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise particular care with stories about suicide and self-harm, considering risk of encouraging others and the feelings of relatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful about presentation, pictures and descriptions of methods — refer to methods in general rather than specific terms where possible. Avoid speculation about a single/simple motive. Avoid images that could act as triggers (places where suicides occurred, scars). Be careful with reporting legal proceedings and inquests; usually not necessary to report every detail. Where appropriate, append helpline notes (Samaritans, local hotlines) and follow Samaritans’ media guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Be tenacious in seeking reliable corroboration of sources; state level of substantiation achieved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take special care verifying online, social media and email sources. Do not state as fact information from someone you cannot authenticate (e.g. use phrasing like “A woman who says she witnessed…”). When relevant, be open about the medium used for an interview (eg via email, Zoom). Desk editors, reporters and subeditors share responsibility for source satisfaction and should challenge dependability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal consultation and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists must familiarise themselves with laws affecting reporting (defamation, privacy, data protection, copyright, contempt, national security) and consult editorial legal when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarise with current state of law in main areas of operation and undertake GNM-provided legal training. Consult in-house or external legal departments or night lawyers in a timely manner before publication on specific legal concerns. Read regular legal notices and complete online legal training when requested. Discuss giving evidence to court with senior editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bribery Act 2010 — payments and hospitality
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware the Bribery Act creates criminal offences for bribery even if committed abroad; offers/acceptance of hospitality or facilitation payments may fall within the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists should be familiar with GNM’s anti-bribery/corruption and gifts/hospitality policies. Discuss beforehand with the relevant senior duty editor if concerned any payments might fall into these categories. Inform the senior duty editor if such payments are requested or made as soon as practicable. There is no public interest defence except in extreme duress situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contempt of court and court reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Take great care when publishing stories that relate to ongoing court cases to avoid prejudicing proceedings; statutory restrictions may apply from time of arrest through trial and appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prejudice could be anything that improperly affects proceedings. Turn off online comments on such stories (exceptions require legal approval). Be wary of jury trials, inquests and crown court matters. Check for automatic statutory restrictions and court orders (family courts, children, vulnerable adults, sexual offences). Contemporaneous, fair and accurate reports of open court generally provide a legal defence, but publishing invasive details may still compromise dignity or privacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyright
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use content (pictures, text, other media) without checking that GNM has the necessary permissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissions include agency content (Reuters, AP) and social media. There are limited legal situations where permission may not be needed — always check with picture desk, senior duty editor or editorial legal before using material without permission. Familiarise with GNM social media guidelines that include copyright sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data protection and the journalism exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: Data protection law governs processing of personal data; the journalism exemption may apply where personal data is processed for journalism with a reasonable belief in public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal data and processing definitions are wide. To rely on the exemption: (1) publication would be in the public interest and (2) complying with usual GDPR/DPA requirements would be incompatible with journalism. Special category data and data about suspected offenders require greater care. For high-profile/intrusive or reputationally damaging stories, keep contemporaneous evidence of decision-making and involve senior duty editor and editorial legal. Always keep personal data secure per GNM InfoSec policy; report potential data incidents promptly to InfoSec, the DPO and editorial legal. If contacted with data access or erasure requests, contact editorial legal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand UK defamation law: claimant must be identifiable, there must be publication, the content must be defamatory and cause/likely cause serious harm; publisher must prove a defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defences include truth, honest opinion, public interest and privilege. The editorial pre-publication right to reply or invitation to comment can be important to a public interest defence. Consider privacy and data protection when weighing defamation/public interest decisions. Editorial legal can advise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy (ECHR article 8 compliance and reasonable expectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect people’s privacy and recognise that potential intrusion must be balanced against the public interest, consistent with article 8 of the ECHR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether there is a reasonable expectation of privacy — a fact-specific inquiry. Celebrities and people in public places, particularly children, may still have a reasonable expectation of privacy. Where an individual has that expectation, journalists must balance freedom of expression against privacy rights and justify any infringement as proportionate. The UK Supreme Court: people under criminal investigation or arrested are considered to have reasonable expectation of privacy until charged and should not generally be named; exceptions require legal approval. Consult senior duty editor and editorial legal where in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should avoid conflicts of interest that could undermine editorial integrity or appear to do so, and should disclose circumstances that may appear to be conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult the managing editor if in doubt. Full transparency is expected; declarations may be required publicly (e.g. end of article or online biography).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial products and promotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not personally endorse commercial products without express permission; declare relationships that could influence coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No Guardian journalist or primary freelance contributor should personally endorse products without express permission from senior editors. Freelancers earning money from a product/brand they write about must declare the relationship in advance and include a footnote acknowledging it. Journalists must not promote financial interests of interviewees or sponsors to secure access. Promotional footnotes should be included only where genuinely of interest to readers. Journalists should not be influenced by commercial considerations (advertisers, affiliate links) in selection/preparation of material. Editorial staff may not work on paid content or advertorials produced by commercial teams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Support good commissioning practice and fair treatment of freelancers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should make reference to GNM’s freelance charter when commissioning contributors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct at work
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent GNM professionally, dress appropriately and be courteous in all exchanges with readers, sources, interviewees, colleagues and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies in person, by telephone, letter, email, online or on social media. Adhere to GNM social media guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality (internal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat personal information about other GNM employees as confidential and do not disclose it except in the course of formal responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain confidentiality for colleagues' personal information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not give subjects the right of copy approval and never offer copy approval as a method of securing interviews or cooperation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In certain circumstances people may be allowed to see quotes to confirm accuracy. Exceptional circumstances permitting advance sight of copy require senior editorial approval and must not be made subject to obligations to alter copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge the source of published material obtained from another organisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit quotes from other newspaper articles and social media. Bylines should be used only on material that is substantially the work of the bylined journalist. If an article contains a significant amount of agency copy, the agency should be credited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations of corporate interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge Guardian Media Group (GMG) relationships and familiarise with GMG companies/interests when reporting on related businesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anyone writing on GMG-related business should seek comments/confirmation in the normal way. Full details of GMG interests are available on the GMG website. Same applies to philanthropic foundations supporting Guardian journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations of personal interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare personal interests or significant connections when writing about related topics; declare to an editor during preparation and potentially in the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: 1) Always declare significant connections to head of department/editor. 2) A connection need not be formal (eg advisory roles require declaration). 3) Obvious connections that justify the commission should be stated at the end of the contribution. 4) Columnists may have more latitude than staff reporters, who should aim for objectivity. 5) Generally, journalists should not commission/write about/quote relatives, partners or close friends; if exception made, make the connection clear. 6) Commissioning editors should ensure freelancers are aware of these rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Report objectively on financial products and avoid using or passing on financial information for personal profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not write about shares in which you or associates have a significant interest or deal in shares you have recently written about. Distinguish clearly between comment, conjecture and fact. Business desk staff must list all shares owned and transactions; maintain and keep up-to-date a register of personal shares. Financial journalists should not be market traders on a regular basis. See Ipso best-practice on financial journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freebies (gifts, hospitality, sponsored trips)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use position to obtain private benefit; gifts/payments must not undermine accuracy, fairness or independence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report attempts to induce favourable editorial treatment to the senior duty editor. Disclose relevant payments/gifts. Footnote when third parties bear travel/accommodation costs; acceptance conditional on GNM being free to assign/report as it sees fit. Do not bring partners/family on free trips unless approved and paid for; return or donate non-perishable gifts over £50. Items supplied for reviews/photo shoots should be returned or stored/donated if impractical to return.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freelance work and media appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: Full-time staff should not contribute to other publications or media without prior authorisation; coordinate media appearances with communications team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staff should talk to the communications team before agreeing to TV/other media appearances to ensure appropriateness and preparedness. Requests to film inside GNM offices must be sent to media.enquiries@theguardian.com for approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: GNM connections (use of position)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use your GNM position to seek personal business/financial advantage or preferential treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use GNM email addresses or social media accounts for non-GNM matters or to cite a Guardian connection to resolve consumer grievances or seek discounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offers of financial assistance to subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not act as intermediaries for donations or fundraising initiatives connected to people featured in Guardian coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not set up crowdfunders connected with Guardian articles and do not link to online fundraising appeals without relevant senior duty editor approval. At most, put willing parties in contact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outside interests and engagements
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare and discuss outside activities that could conflict with professional duties, particularly political involvement and paid/unpaid roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss with editor-in-chief/US/Australia editor/managing editor before: working for a political party or campaign role; outside employment likely to conflict; giving evidence to court; making representations to official bodies about GNM material; chairing/speaking at public events as a GNM journalist. If an event is approved, do not accept payment for events during work hours (travel/expenses ok). Fees for significant private-time commitments may be accepted with prior approval. Never provide public relations advice. Declare relevant personal/financial interests on online biographies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payments for stories and using external agents
rubrics_metrics.description: GNM does not pay sources or interviewees except in rare approved circumstances; approval required for paying or using external non-journalistic agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any exceptions require relevant senior duty editor approval. Journalists should not engage paid external non-journalistic agents/assistants without prior knowledge and approval. On occasion GNM may pay tip fees to bona fide freelance journalists. See clause 15 on witness payments in criminal trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationships and editorial decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should not generally commission, write about, photograph, film or make editorial decisions about individuals with whom they have a close personal or financial relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a relationship with a public figure or journalist (inside or outside GNM) creates a potential conflict of interest and discuss with the managing editor. If an exception is made, the connection should be made clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media conduct (professionalism and safety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat people with respect and professionalism on social media and use common sense before posting, recognising that private posts can be shared publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Familiarise with GNM’s full social media guidelines and the 'staying safe online' document. Always adhere to these and think twice before posting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source care and protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand practicalities and limitations of protecting sources; do not promise outcomes beyond GNM’s control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend GNM editorial legal and InfoSec training on source protection; consult InfoSec to ensure technology/software up to date; familiarise with secure contact methods (eg SecureDrop). Electronic devices must comply with GNM InfoSec encryption standards. In addition to digital measures, meeting in person or using post/hand delivery may be appropriate.
